messages.author: عبد الرحمن الجزائري
text:
If you want to teach a child something, you must first understand it yourself. Not at the level of a scholar, but enough to give a mental model—a framework.

Don't dump details on children, plant seeds instead.

Children's minds are fertile soil. That's why they sometimes shock us with sharp observations. It's not magic. It's a fresh brain working from the roots up, without layers of bad assumptions.

When you notice that spark, stop and pay attention. That's a blessing. Grow it. Watch the questions they ask. Those questions are the mind revealing how it works and what it needs to reach its potential.

People are different, and children are people. Intelligence is not one thing.

When a child asks something you cannot answer, do not improvise nonsense. That kills curiosity, because the child senses that. It's like pouring water on a flame.

Say clearly: "I don't know. I'll ask someone knowledgeable". Or: "Let's do a research about it!", but only if you are qualified. Otherwise ask people who are.

That does something powerful. The spark stays alive. It intensifies. The child waits, thinks, anticipates. Sometimes they solve it themselves through logic. Sometimes they learn something deeper: this question matters. It’s big enough that even mommy or daddy must ask others.

Let them feel that. They need it.

That's how you grow a healthy plant. Later, it becomes a tree. Trees give fruit. Fruit carries seeds.

Do not limit the child. Teach them that knowledge is vast, and that scholars exist for a reason.

text: بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

The Prophet ﷺ did not teach us to do this, therefore it is not a Sunnah.

When we look to the Sahaba رضي الله عنهم, we find that they did not practice this, nor did the generations after them, such as the Tabi‘een رحمهم الله. This shows that it is not the way of those who preceded us.

Furthermore, this practice is not found in any of the books of fiqh.

A bid‘ah is an innovation that is introduced into the Deen without precedent and is connected to an act of ‘ibaadah.
Based on this, it is considered a bid‘ah.

text:
Example

A small child asks al-Albānī

Abū Laylā: Ask the Shaykh quickly… a small question, O Shaykh.

The child: O Shaykh, did the Messenger of Allah, did he herd sheep?

The Shaykh: The Messenger of Allah, what?

Abū Laylā: Did he herd sheep? Say, ﷺ.

The child: ﷺ, did he herd sheep?

The Shaykh: Yes, he herded sheep. And he, ’alayhi as-salām said:
"And there is no prophet except that he herded sheep".

Abū Laylā: May Allah reward you.

The Shaykh: And you as well.


Source:

Notice how persistent he is, while still following guidance from Abū Laylā. He keeps calling the sheikh "Yā sheikh, yā sheikh".
He knows his answer lies within this sheikh.

messages.author: عبد الرحمن الجزائري
text:
Text flattens people.

It carries ideas, but it does not carry voice, pauses, or facial cues. What would sound calm and welcoming in speech can appear sharp once written, even when the intent is unchanged.

This is clearer in technical discussions. Clear conclusions and direct reasoning often read louder between letters than they do in real conversation.

Certainty, in text, is easily mistaken for harshness, arrogance, being a "know-it-all". That is not always a matter of character; often it is a property of the medium itself.

People also differ in how they communicate. Some prefer a gradual, softened approach. Others state the conclusion plainly and then walk through the reasoning. These are methods, and they reflect style, not the state of a person's heart.

It helps to keep things from getting mixed, to realize that:
* An argument is weighed by its evidence.
* Tone shapes how that argument is received in a given context.
* Intentions, however, are not visible to others. Those belong to a different domain altogether, and they are known only to Allāh.

So when something written feels firm, understand that firmness is directed at ideas, not at people. And when words come across sharper than intended, that is often a limitation of text, not a reflection of character.

Allāh knows best.

text.text: ليس كل العلم ينشر | Not every knowledge should be spread

text: When we share knowledge (of our dīn) we must look at the harms and benefits that will come about—

.

Some masāʾil should be left from speaking about to the public. It is from ʿilm that you look to who you are speaking and addressing. 

As an example, praying in shoes is from the Sunnah. However, mentioning this to the general public without ḥikmah may lead to harm. People may begin praying in the masjid with dirty shoes, which could cause others to be repelled from the coming to the masjid and say, “They claim to follow the Sunnah, yet they dirty the house of Allāh.”

There is a genuine concern when it comes to spreading knowledge and fear of concealing it [

]; but the ʿulemāʾ placed a criterion on spreading knowledge—between not spreading every bit of it and not withholding all of it. 

In Islām, prevention of corruption is given precedence over bringing benefit to prevent corruption being spread out by way of this (even if there is benefit in sharing it). 

Ash-Shāṭibī رحمه الله said: “Not every knowledge should be spread/broadcasted. Even if it is true.” 

He also added that Imām Mālik mentioned that he has many aḥadīth which he did not speak about nor did he relay it to anyone else—this is because he disliked any speech with no action that comes from it.
“وكان يكره الكلام فيما ليس تحته عمل"
[الموافقات ١٧١:٥]

The criterion the ʿulemāʾ say to use is to present the issue to the Shari’ah. If it is sound according to its scale, then look at its context regarding the state and era of the people—this requires ʿilm and ḥikmah; wisdom which can only be obtained by experience.

There is also the issue of
the knowledge is shared—the
in which it is conveyed; which is another discussion.

“وكان يكره الكلام فيما ليس تحته عمل"
[الموافقات ١٧١:٥]

The criterion the ʿulemāʾ say to use is to present the issue to the Shari’ah. If it is sound according to its scale, then look at its context regarding the state and era of the people—this requires ʿilm and ḥikmah; wisdom which can only be obtained by experience.

There is also the issue of
how
the knowledge is shared—the
way
in which it is conveyed; which is another discussion.

An excerpt from my notes of  الطريق إلى النبوغ العلمي taught by Ustādh Abū Hudhayfa Sāmī حفظه الله 

~ أم مصعب الغانية الألمانية

text.text: Am I missing out on my youth because I wear the niqāb?

text:
بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم 

As Muslims, we strive to live by the Qur’ān and Sunnah. 
When we cover ourselves, we are living by an āyah of the Qur’ān.

text.text: We are striving to resemble the ṣaḥābiyyāt رضي الله عنهن

text:
– and what an honour and immense niʿmah it is that Allāh grants a servant the tawfīq to obey Him in this way.🍯

✽  Many of the doubts that arise around the niqāb are forms of
, catered to one’s weaknesses.

text.text: Shayṭān does not attempt to divert a person through things that hold no weight with them

text: ; rather, he targets what already tugs at the heart and the closer one draws to Allāh, the more these whispers may appear - as well as outside noise from others questioning your decision.

text.text: When such thoughts arise, it is important to pause and ask:

text:
Where is this coming from?
Is it your environment?
The people you surround myself with?
The content you consume?

For many sisters today, social media and modern influences play a major role in shaping how we perceive ourselves and our lives (unfortunately). Over time, these influences subtly redefine our standards, and even our understanding of ‘youth’. 

✿

text.text: Preserving one’s dīn sometimes requires distancing oneself from that which weakens it

text:
– and if removing certain influences is a means of preservation, then it is a step worth taking for the sake of Allāh.

🔑As Muslims, we do not define our ‘youth’ by society’s standards, we define it by what pleases Allāh سبحانه وتعالى

✽  The concept of ‘youth’ itself is subjective. For some, youth is defined by partying, relationships, and time wasted in matters displeasing to Allāh. For others, youth is a opportunity to draw closer to Allāh, hoping to be among those whom the Prophet صلى الله عليه وسلم mentioned as being shaded on the Day of Judgement

. 

As a Muslimah, the latter is the one you should strive for and find contentment in

✿  Equating the niqāb with ‘missing out on your youth’ reflects a misunderstanding of its premise.

text.text: Concealing one’s beauty does not mean erasing it.

text: Rather, it means knowing when, where, and to whom it is revealed.

text.text: You are not missing out on your youth or your femininity by choosing to reveal your beauty to those whom Allāh has permitted, while concealing it from those He has not.

It's not ḥarām for us to beautify ourselves but it's just that we do within the safe spaces – and those spaces are defined by الله سبحانه وتعالى

✽

text:
Allowing other people’s opinions to define what ‘missing out’ means, only opens the door to further waswās - especially when one already feels tempted toward displaying their beauty. 

Such thoughts often stem from the following claim :

. Sometimes we say things to comfort ourselves and justify our actions - even when we know they’re wrong: however, ask yourself:
Would I still do this if no one saw me?
Who is this really for?
Am I really doing this for myself alone, or am I doing it due to external influence?

✿  If beautification and adornment are things you enjoy then that is natural and you should embrace it! Allow yourself to acknowledge your beauty
it to the acceptance of others - and know it is not something you

, rather make it something you choose to do in order to enhance your natural beauty which Allāh granted you 

Redirect them to be among your sisters, within private spaces, or that which is greater:

text.text: for your husband - in which there is great reward.

text: If approval and praise are what your heart seeks, then seek them from those whom Allāh has permitted🪷

messages.text:
“O my father, hire him” meaning, seek him for me as a husband.

So take active but dignified steps, through righteous sisters, students of knowledge, or those you trust, to find a man known for his religion and character.

And also do not close your heart to polygyny, if a righteous man who is already married proposes. Perhaps Allaah has written for you comfort and balance in such a situation, a husband who divides his time between homes may give you ample time to continue your studies. Thus, you combine two blessings: serving your husband and remaining diligent in seeking knowledge.

Always renew your intention and say:


{ وَٱلَّذِینَ یَقُولُونَ رَبَّنَا هَبۡ لَنَا مِنۡ أَزۡوَ ٰ⁠جِنَا وَذُرِّیَّـٰتِنَا قُرَّةَ أَعۡیُنࣲ وَٱجۡعَلۡنَا لِلۡمُتَّقِینَ إِمَامًا (74) }
[Surah Al-Furqān: 72-74]
And those who say: Our Lord! Bestow on us from our wives and our offspring the comfort of our eyes, and make us leaders of the Muttaqûn(the pious. See V.{2:2}).


And remember, my noble sister, that the true fruit of knowledge is action and tranquility, not just lessons or memorization. There is no worship more beloved to Allaah than that which builds a righteous home and raises believing children who will carry the religion after us, especially for a woman.

Thus, continue seeking knowledge, but make it a means, not an end, and work toward opening the door of marriage, for it is an easier and more certain path to Allaah’s pleasure when fulfilled as He commanded.

May Allaah open your chest, increase you in beneficial knowledge, make you steadfast upon righteousness, bless you with a righteous and knowledge loving husband, a scholar, a worshipper, who will be a source of comfort in this world and your companion in Jannah.

والله أعلم 

With love from your sister
Ummu Hayaa Haleemah An-Nījīrīyah 
Ummu Hayaa's Majlis

Date Asked:
9 Rabi'ul Awwal (3) 1447 
 29 October (10) 2025

Date Answered:
10 Rabi'ul Awwal (3) 1447 
 30 October (10) 2025

messages.text:
السلام عليكم ورحمة الله وبركاته

A short piece on teaching children in harmony with their fitrah.

messages.text:
How many times have you read a benefit on your device and it was a cause for you to stop scrolling?

The best amongst us scroll on our devices reading "benefit" after "benefit", which is a scary, because that which you have read will either be for you or against you on the day of account.

Are we accumulating good deeds by scrolling or are we causing our own destruction?!.

Subhanallah, who would of ever thought just a flick of a thumb or finger could be a means of ones destruction and failure.

وصية الإمام سفيان الثوري رحمه الله:

"يا بني، إذا كتبت عشرة أحاديث -وفي رواية: عشرة أحرف- فانظر هل ترى في نفسك زيادة في مشيك وحلمك ووقارك؟ فإن لم تَرَ ذلك فاعلم أنه يضرك ولا ينفعك"

 (تاريخ جرجان للسهمي؛ ص: [449-450]، الترجمة رَقْم: [997]، وصفة الصفوة).

Advice from the mother of Imam Sufyān al-Thawri to sufyān رحمه الله:

"O my son, if you write ten hadiths — and in another narration: ten letters — then observe whether you see an increase in your manner of walking, your forbearance, and your dignity. If you do not see that, then know that it harms you and does not benefit you."

(History of Jurjan by al-Sahmi; pp. [449-450], biography no. [997], and Sifat al-Safwa).



And we say:
Every "benefit" you read through these groups/online, observe whether you have gained closer to Allāh or not, if not, then know it has done more harm to you than good.

Apart from time, this is one of the reasons why I don't post much, alot of what is posted is forgotten by the sender and the reader, the most that could be said was: "I remember seeing this benefit somewhere online"

To truly benefit online, this requires great understanding, the correct methodology, strong emān to ward of desires, and firm knowledge to ward of doubts and Allah's help is sought.

ولا حول ولا قوة إلا بالله

messages.author: عبد الرحمن الجزائري
text:
I don't like the tone of that post, but the idea behind the tone is correct, and it's this one: Stop accumulating knowledge like accumulation itself is the goal. The goal is practice.

I once wrote about it, and said:

text.text:
Something that helps making this happen is studying only what matters to you at the moment, what you need in your actual life currently, so you could live according to what Allāh wants from us.
Don't go about seeking knowledge like you're pursuing an academic diploma. Please. You'll just end up piling information.  That's how theory overwhelms practice. Which is one of the reasons I hate academic systems.

Remember how the companions learned 10 āyāt at once. Somehow, almost everyone simply ignores that method, and just goes about memorizing so many things and delving into issues that they're far from needing them anytime soon.

Perhaps that's why we have a character crisis. Too much theory hardens the heart, and poofs one up like a balloon.

It's sad. But it is true.

text:
It's also the advice of al-Albāny, when he gets asked, how should a knowledge seeker start? His answer: By priority.

Meaning: What matters most for him in his life as a Muslim. Not what's interesting. Not what's impressive. What's obligatory and relevant.

So the question shouldn't be: how many benefits did you read?
It should be: how many of them touched your actual practice?

What we have online is massive noise and weak signal. A better model would be to stop dumping information and instead share lived practice—what we're dealing with, applying, failing at—along with the relevant material. That alone would cut most of the noise.

It also helps to remember that many knowledge seekers online have little guidance and limited grounding, but a lot of zeal. That combination produces over-posting and overconsumption. 

People need to choose carefully whom they follow. Not everyone fits everyone. Stick with those you naturally resonate with. Narrowing is clarity, not loss.

Following countless channels just to make your feed feel "alive" (whether consciously or not) isn't healthy.

I personally keep my feed very curated, and to a lot, it seems dry. I like it that way.

messages.text:
I would like to also point out a connection that makes sense:

The advice about ten  "hadīths" or "letters" is almost certainly a practical adaptation of the principle behind the companions' method of ten āyāt.

Sufyān's mother was teaching him the same logic: start small, internalize, observe the effect on character and practice, not volume.

Why? I'd say so he wouldn't fall into mere accumulation like so many others do, in their time.

It's a beautiful example of transmission: the method survives, even if the units (āyāt, letters, hadiths) vary.

Hah! Perhaps we should do ten benefits at a time. Don't move on until you absorb their value.

text.text: And whenever there comes down a Sūrah (chapter from the Qur’ān), some of them (hypocrites) say: Which of you has had his Faith increased by it? As for those who believe, it has increased their Faith, and they rejoice

text:
[At-Tawbah 9:124].
Tr. Muhsin Khan and Taqi-ud-Din al-Hilali

Tafsīr as-Sa‘dī:

text.text:
Allah describes the state of the hypocrites and the believers when the Qur’ān is revealed, and the difference between the two groups. He says:

"Whenever a sūrah is revealed" containing commands, prohibitions, knowledge of Allāh and the unwitnessed, and exhortation to jihād.

"some of them say: Which of you has had his Faith increased by it?" — a question that arose concerning whose faith truly increased among the two groups.

Allāh, Exalted is He, makes clear the state of the affair: "As for those who believe, it has increased them in faith" through knowledge of it, understanding it, believing it, acting upon it, desiring good, and refraining from evil.

"And they rejoice", meaning, they greet each other with glad tidings of what Allāh has granted them through His āyāt, and the success to understand and act upon them. This indicates the comfort of their chests by the āyāt of Allāh, the reassurance of their hearts, and their readiness to obey what the Qur’ān urges them to do.

text: «تاريخ الإسلام - ط التوفيقية» (31/ 73):

text.text:
وقال بركة بْن محمد الحلبي: كنَّا عند بقيّة في غُرْفة، فسمع الناس يقولون: لا لا، فأخرج رأسه مِن الطاقة وجعل يصيح معهم: لا لا؛ فقلنا: يا أبا يُحمد، سبحان الله، أنت إمام يُقتدَى بك.
قَالَ: أُسْكُتْ هذه سُنَّة بلدنا.

text: «Tārīkh al-Islām – at-Tawfīqiyyah edition» (31/73):

text.text:
Barakah ibn Muḥammad al-Ḥalabī said: We were with Baqiyyah in a room, when he heard people saying, "No! No!". So he stuck his head out of the window and began shouting with them: "No! No!".

We said: O Abā Yuḥmid, subḥāna Allāh, you are an imām whom people take as an example.

He replied: Be quiet! This is the custom of our town.

text: I want friends like Baqqiyah…

text.text:
وقال عطيّة بْن بقيّة: قَالَ أَبِي: دخلت على الرشيد، 
[...]
قَالَ: فامتلأ مِن ذَلِكَ فرحًا وقال: يا غلام، ناولني الدَّوَاة. وكان القيّم بأمره الفضل بْن الربيع ومرتبته بُعَيْدَة، فناداني وقال: يا بقيّة، ناوِلْ أمير المؤمنين الدَّواة بجانبك.
قلت: ناوِلْه أنت يا هامان.
فقال: سَمِعْتُ ما قَالَ لي يا أمير المؤمنين؟ قَالَ: اسكتْ، فما كنت عنده هامان حتّى أكون عنده فرعون.

text: «Tārīkh al-Islām – at-Tawfīqiyyah edition» (31/73):

text.text:
ʿAṭiyyah ibn Baqiyyah said: My father said: I entered upon ar-Rashīd,
[…]
He said: He became filled with joy because of that and said: "Boy, hand me the inkwell".

The one in charge of his affairs was al-Faḍl ibn ar-Rabīʿ, and he was just a bit far, so he called out to me and said: "O Baqiyyah, hand Amīr al-Muʾminīn the inkwell beside you".

I said: "You hand it to him, O Hāmān".

He said: "Did you hear what he said to me, O Amīr al-Muʾminīn?"

He [the caliph] replied: "Be quiet. He would not consider you Hāmān unless He considered me Firʿawn (Pharaoh)".

text: Baqiyyah was courageous and bold, and Hāroon ar-Rashīd was VERY clement and merciful. He loved scholars and respected them a lot.

text.text: For indeed, With Hardship Comes Ease; Indeed, With Hardship Comes Ease

text:
A promise from your Rabb—who has neither forsaken you nor abandoned you.

What you are feeling is only a product of your own weakness, and that weakness itself is proof of the hardship you are going through.

So take this as a good sign, seek Allāh's forgiveness, await relief, and strive toward it.

Your Lord has promised you two eases, and no single hardship can ever overcome two eases.

Be patient, and have patience. Console your soul with the sweetness of relief, and know that its sweetness is in proportion to the bitterness of your patience.

Be like a sick person who swallows bitter medicine, certain that Allāh has placed in it a cause for healing.

Be like the woman seized by labor, striving to bring her child into the world, enduring the pain while being certain that Allāh will unite her with her child.

Do not allow your thoughts to wander into the labyrinths of "what if?!". Turn away from them and have good expectations of your Rabb.

Do not deal with your Rabb as you deal with humans, who are weak. Your Rabb is the Owner of everything; He does whatever He wills.

All that is required of you is to obey your Rabb, turn away from disobedience, and abandon it. If that is so, then Allāh has indeed promised you ease after hardship—ease after hardship.

Written by ʿAbdu ar-Raḥmān al-Qaddārī, emulating the style of ash-shaykh ʿAmmār al-Ḥawbānī.

text: I would like to address a misconception that some knowledge seekers seem to have, which is:

text.text: Poor life quality means knowledge attainment.

text: Or:

text.text: If I'm eating well and having a soft bed and so on, I won't be able to attain knowledge.

text: Some quote this:

text.text:
It was narrated (to us) Yahyā bnu Yahyā at-Tamīmī (who) said: ‘Abdullāh bnu Yahyā bnu Abī Kathīr said: "I heard my father say:

'Knowledge is not obtained with the relaxation of the body'".

[Sahīh Muslim (612)

text:
This is wrong.

You can still eat well everyday.

The relaxation meant in the report is not about food quality, it's about the effort spent to seek knowledge.

Al-imām Muslim reported that in his Saḥīḥ after he had spent immense effort on a ḥadīth. 

What you might find about hardships faced by scholars is merely circumstances. It's not necessary. As many scholars had a luxurious life, like al-Layth ibnu Saʿd. He's an imām.

They just didn't let their wealth and dunyā get in the way of spending effort in seeking knowledge.

What you might find about hardships faced by scholars is merely circumstances. It's not necessary. As many scholars had a luxurious life, like al-Layth ibnu Saʿd. He's an imām.

They just didn't let their wealth and dunyā get in the way of spending effort in seeking knowledge.

text:
Write. Publish. Share. On blogs.
Don't rely only on just Telegram or similar enclosed platforms.

? Because search engines don't pick up Telegram content the way they do blog posts. A lot of people search for answers online, and mostly, they find deviant Islamic websites.

That's why we need to put more effort into websites and blogs. That's how we actually compete with the people of falsehood; not by joining Instagram, Facebook, or the worst of all: TikTok.
عياذا بالله.

Instead of pulling people out of these harmful platforms, we've dragged ourselves in.
سبحان الله.

Not many people know how to search the internet properly. Even fewer know where to find credible sources. "Look, I just Googled this fatwā, and that's enough for me". Sound familiar?

Yes, posting on Telegram is easier. But the benefits of using websites and blogs far outweigh the friction. It's not even close.

Start simple. Blogger (Blogspot). Over time, you can explore WordPress or other platforms.

Take the space, occupy the search results, and compete where it actually matters.

Your blog post today could still be educating someone ten years from now. A Telegram post doesn't have the same chance, because it's linear.

text: Someone mentioned this athar of imām Mālik رحمه الله:

text.text:
«إِنَّ هَذَا الْأَمْرَ لَنْ يُنَالَ حَتَّى يُذَاقَ فِيهِ طَعْمُ الْفَقْرِ»
"This matter (knowledge) will not be attained until one tastes, within it, the flavour of poverty".

text: This does

mean that poverty is a condition for attaining knowledge.

If the statement were taken as absolute, it would contradict clear realities:
ʿUthmān and ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān bnu ʿAwf رضي الله عنهما were wealthy and among the most knowledgeable of this Ummah.
Likewise Ibn Sīrīn, Saʿīd bnu al-Musayyib, Abū Ḥanīfah, Ibn al-Mubārak, al-Layth bnu Saʿd, and others.

What imām Mālik is pointing to is something commonly observed, not a requirement: many scholars happened to be poor, largely because wealth often distracts people. This makes wealthy scholars

, not the opposite.

So:
* Poverty is not a condition.
* Richness does not lower one's rank.
* One should not remain poor, or make himself poor, thinking this is necessary for knowledge.
* Nor should wealthy students be looked down upon as missing a key ingredient.

It is not binary.

The Prophet ﷺ did not command poverty, nor did the companions understand wealth to be blameworthy in itself. Some were given abundance, some sufficiency: each according to what suited them.

What matters is effort, discipline, and that dunyā does not dominate the heart.

Eating well is not the problem. Becoming lazy is.

Allāh knows best.
May Allāh reward who brought this to our attention.

text: Umm al-Faḍl — the wife of Shaykh al-Albānī رحمه الله — was asked:

text.text: “Being the wife of this virtuous scholar, have you found that his knowledge, his seeking of knowledge, and his teaching of people reduced his presence with you as the head of your household? And did this have any negative effect on his children?”

text:
she responded: "seeking knowledge never prevented the Shaykh from fulfilling any of his family duties. On the contrary, he—may Allah have mercy on him—was an example of a head of household who cooperated with his family.

Believe me, my son, he would often help me with the household chores to the point that I would feel shy because of it. He even once was mopping the balcony with me, and I said to him: “Shaykh, don’t embarrass us in front of the neighbors, lest they say this man does his wife’s work.” He replied: “This is not an embarrassment. Do you not know that the Prophet ﷺ used to serve his family?”

Whenever I asked him for anything related to the house—such as installing an extra shelf somewhere—he would study the matter and think about it. If he saw the request as reasonable, he would go ahead and do it himself. And if he needed to buy something for it, he would go in his car, purchase it, return, and carry out what I had pointed out to him.

He also had a fondness for outings—may Allah have mercy on him—the way of ahlul shām. The picnic basket (the outing supplies) was always in the car. We would go out together in spring and summer, and even in winter, to look at the snow and the winter scenery. He would humor me by drinking tea and coffee, even though he did not personally enjoy these two beverages. 

Yet he would never leave his books behind on any outing we took; the book was his companion wherever he went.

Often, I would wake up and not find him in bed. I would look for him and find him in the library, having turned on the lamp and become immersed in his books. I would be surprised, and he would say: “This is my beloved!!” — may Allah have mercy on him."

may Allah have mercy on them both.

text.text:
5954) ʿAlī bnu ʿAbdillāh narrated to us; Sufyān narrated to us; he said: I heard ʿAbdurraḥmān bnu al-Qāsim—there was no one in Madīnah at that time better than him—say: I heard my father say: I heard ʿĀʾishah, may Allāh be pleased with her, say:
The Messenger of Allāh, ṣallallāhu ʿalayhi wa-sallam, returned from a journey, and I had covered a niche of mine with a thin curtain that had figures on it. When the Messenger of Allāh, ṣallallāhu ʿalayhi wa-sallam, saw it, he tore it and said: "The most severely punished on the Day of Resurrection are those who imitate the [act of] creation of Allāh".
She said: So we turned it into a cushion, or two.

text:
her statement: "he tore it"

So, my brothers in Īmān—those who take the Messenger of Allāh, ṣallallāhu ʿalayhi wa-sallam, as their example—those who wipe only the face and leave the head; those who treat images gently, softly, leniently; those who do not feel the reprehensibility of those images: Obliterate every image, without leaving a trace.

What benefit is that image? Why expose yourself to the Fire of Jahannam? What wisdom is there in that? (A rhetorical question, of course).

Think about it. Imagine you were living in the time of the Messenger, ṣallallāhu ʿalayhi wa-sallam, and he saw you wiping only the face, keeping it with you, and displaying it openly.

لا إله إلا الله.

text.text: A Translator Is The Author, The Translator, And The Reader

text:
A translator occupies three minds at once: the author's, their own, and the reader's.

You read a sentence. You feel what the author felt. You hear their intention. You judge how the reader will receive it. You read it from the other side. You feel how it lands.

Every word, every pause, every rhythm is on the line.

{ ۞ وَمَن یُهَاجِرۡ فِی سَبِیلِ ٱللَّهِ یَجِدۡ فِی ٱلۡأَرۡضِ مُرَ ٰ⁠غَمࣰا كَثِیرࣰا وَسَعَةࣰۚ وَمَن یَخۡرُجۡ مِنۢ بَیۡتِهِۦ مُهَاجِرًا إِلَى ٱللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِۦ ثُمَّ یُدۡرِكۡهُ ٱلۡمَوۡتُ فَقَدۡ وَقَعَ أَجۡرُهُۥ عَلَى ٱللَّهِۗ وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ غَفُورࣰا رَّحِیمࣰا }
[سُورَةُ النِّسَاءِ: ١٠٠]

He who emigrates (from his home) in the Cause of Allâh, will find on earth many dwelling places and plenty to live by. And whosoever leaves his home as an emigrant unto Allâh and His Messenger, and death overtakes him, his reward is then surely incumbent upon Allâh. And Allâh is Ever Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.

Tr. Muhsin Khan and Taqi-ud-Din al-Hilali

text.text: هل تصبر طالبة العلم وترفض الخطاب إلى أن يتقدم إليها طالب علم؟

السؤال: امرأة طالبة علم، ويتقدم اليها الخطاب، ولكنهم ليسوا بطلاب علم. فبعض الأحيان والداها يرضان بغير طالب العلم، والمرأة ترفض وتريد طالب علم. 

فما نصيحتكم؟

الشيخ يحيى الحجوري: لها الحق…أن تصبر حتى يتيسر لها من ترضى دينه، وترضى استقامته، وكونه كذلك طالب علم.

فإن هذه حياة:
* إن يسر الله مثلا فيها تطاوع، حصل فيها السعادة وراحة النفس، والتطاوع والصبر والعيشة الطيبة.
* وإن حصل فيها العجلة، وحصل فيها، كما يقال، عدم التأني، ربما وقع الإنسان - بعد تقدير الله عز وجل - بما لا يرضاه، فيما لا يرضاه، ومصير ذلك للفراق، إذا حصل سوء حال، ويكون ربما غير مستقيم...وإن كان في بداية الأمر قد ربما يقول "لعله ولعله"، فلا شك أن الاستقامة فضلها عظيم.

فلا بأس بالتأني، ويُنْصَحُون بذلك، حتى ييسر الله طلاب العلم الأفاضل [وهم] كثير. ولطالب علم فاضل، حتى وإن حصل شيء من الصبر من المدة، أو امرأة طالبة علم فاضلة، خير من الاستعجال، كما سبق.

text.text: Should a female knowledge seeker be patient and refuse proposals until a knowledge seeker proposes to her?

The question:
A woman who is a student of knowledge receives marriage proposals, but the men who propose are not. At times, her parents are content with such a person, while the woman refuses and wishes to marry a student of knowledge.

So what is your advice?

Shaykh Yaḥyā al-Ḥajūrī:
She has the right… to be patient until Allāh facilitates for her someone whose religion she is pleased with, whose uprightness she is pleased with, and who is likewise a student of knowledge.

For this is a life:

If Allāh facilitates, for example, mutual accord within it, then happiness is attained, along with peace of mind, mutual harmony, patience, and a wholesome life.

But if haste occurs, and what is called a lack of deliberation occurs, then perhaps a person—after the decree of Allāh, ʿazza wa jall—ends up in circumstances he is not pleased with, and in a condition he finds unsatisfactory, and that may ultimately lead to separation, should circumstances deteriorate; and he may be someone lacking uprightness… even if, at the beginning, one might say, “perhaps this, perhaps that”. There is no doubt that uprightness has tremendous virtue.

So there is no harm in deliberation, and they should be advised to that, until Allāh facilitates virtuous knowledge seeker—and they are many. And a virtuous knowledge seeker, even if some patience over a period of time is required, or a virtuous female knowledge seeker, is better than haste, as mentioned previously.

messages.author: عبد الرحمن الجزائري
text:
“بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم
السلام عليكم ورحمة الله وبركاته

الله يحفظكم

This is a response to the ongoing discussion regarding the posting of marriage profiles on this channel.

Firstly, it is important to return to the fatwā of Shaykh ʿAbdul-Ḥamīd az-Zuʿkarī حفظه الله, where he stated that such a service is permissible as long as it remains safe from fitnah. This condition is very important and cannot be overlooked. As many sisters have pointed out, there are real and valid concerns about the fitnah that can come from making personal marriage details public. These concerns should not be brushed aside in the name of a “greater good” or ease.

The Sharīʿah does not allow us to seek benefit while opening doors to harm, especially when the matter involves marriage and the stability of Muslim homes.

It is reported that the Prophet ﷺ said that Shayṭān places his throne upon the water and sends out his troops, and that the closest to him are those who cause the greatest tribulation — particularly the one who separates a man from his wife (Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim). None of us would wish to unintentionally assist Shayṭān in this, yet it is undeniable that public profiles can open doors that may aid in this. Even if some marriages are facilitated, others may be harmed in the process, even if that harm is unintentional. This is not a discouragement from doing good, but a call to seek safer and more protective means.

Secondly, marriage is a form of rizq. What Allāh has decreed will reach a person regardless of the method used. Many people have utilised public matrimonial profiles and channels for years and remain unmarried, while numerous Telegram channels still have profiles dating back to their initial launch — Masjid al-Istiqāmah being one example. Even if it is argued that some people got married and forgot to remove their profiles, this only shows that the marriage did not occur because of the profile being publicly available, as profiles are removed once a match is made. This itself demonstrates that public exposure is neither a guarantee nor a necessity for marriage. Therefore, those who choose not to engage in this method are not placing themselves in “unnecessary hardship”. Provision does not come from visibility; it comes from Allāh.

If that is the case, then why not seek marriage through what is more dignified, more protective, and closer to the Sunnah?

Thirdly, the idea of public profiles comes from kuffār dating systems. Marriage in Islām is sacred. Even if someone argues that profiles are technically permissible, imitating such systems in something as serious as marriage should make us pause. Barakah is not only sought in the outcome, but also in the way something is done.

Ahl al-Sunnah are people of tamyīz — distinction. Our concern is not merely that marriage happens, but how it happens. We choose what is better, more honourable, and more protective of the hearts and homes of the believers. Ease should never come at the expense of principles. Everyone seeks marriage — the kuffār and the people of bidʿah included — but are they seeking it with the same concern for barakah and sound means?

Since this initiative is mainly aimed at students of knowledge, we should not rely on statements such as “this shaykh said” or “that teacher allowed” as a shield. The shuyūkh will still receive a reward if they erred, but that does not apply to us. If something appears to resemble the ways of the people of fisq or kufr, then leaving it — out of waraʿ and caution — is more befitting, even if others have not deemed it impermissible.

The Prophet ﷺ advised us to leave what causes doubt for what does not cause doubt. This principle alone is enough for the one who wants safety.

This is what Allāh has made easy for me to mention, and I hope it is of benefit.

May Allāh grant us sincerity, guide us to what pleases Him, and place barakah in every effort taken upon His dīn.”

messages.text:
الله أكبر!

اللهم بارك!

She has articulated it in an amazing manner.

اللهم بارك.

Point by point, you think she's done...and nope, there's more akhi.
Allow me to break your idea of permissibility!

الحمد لله.

I personally, instinctively, felt uncomfortable regarding public profiles. People look like merchandise...really.

It strips away the dignity in a horrible way. Think about it. A profile of a sister publicly for everyone to see? No matter how "private" you think the profile is!

Remember, always remember: technology is merely a tool to accomplish what we've already known and done.

In real life, do we publicly announce a woman's profile in banners and at the masjid's doors?
Do we make an announcement in newspapers?

"If you're interested, call us using this phone number".

Just...no...

We do it privately, the woman is treated as a queen, because she is!

We preserve her, keep her dignified, highly respected! That's the core of your future family!

Her wali is her guardian, her protector. He's a human being who has contacts, use that!

We're like a hive of bees, connected! Let your neighboring bees know you want a good bee to marry (lol, sorry).

Don't go outside of the nest and shout at everyone to hear, including the nest of wasps next doors....(ugh).

والله أعلم.

Sorry if I went overboard. But I hate the idea of public profiles.

May Allāh reward the sister for that answer, it helped me structure why I disagree with the idea.

text.text: A Woman's Beauty is Like a Rose

text:
🌹

Stunningly lovely, but it develops in certain stages. It has a finite window, and is on a very specific timer. 

Just as a rose is initially a tiny flower bud that is tightly closed, then begins to slowly open over time and then blossom into full-blown loveliness, then its full bloom eventually droops with age and then dies:

Feminine physical beauty follows a similar trajectory and is similarly tied to the concept of time. 

Young ladies, your biggest and most time-sensitive assests are your youth and your beauty. 

Not your degrees, not your money, not your career.

I know it sounds jarring to our modern ears because it's not politically correct to state this truth bluntly anymore because modern feminists suppress it. But it's the basic reality of things, and all traditional past societies used to know it. 

Ladies, don't waste this natural femininity on extended higher education or a collection of secular degrees or a fixation on a "career." Similarly, don't waste your time "talking to" a guy who isn't serious or intending marriage, no matter what lies he tells you or what compliments he flatters you with or what cheesy pick-up lines he uses on you. 

This all wastes a lot of your time. Time you can't get back. 

Instead of squandering your precious beauty and youth on what western feminists say, capitalize on those natural blessings by marrying a righteous husband and starting a beautiful family at your prime. Do what your heart desires, in the halal way. 

Don't delay your own happiness for silly reasons. Later in life, many older women come to regret not having enjoyed their femininity and the youthful energy of their prime years in the context of young love and early marriage, and lament having suppressed their own joy and femininity to pursue decades of useless western degrees and an unfulfilling job they hate. 

Muslim parents, please don't fabricate excuses or create barriers to your daughter getting married. Don't make up reasons for why your daughter can't get married now at 19, 20, or 21 and mature and responsible, because you insist that she needs to finish her education or get a career or become "established" before even thinking about marriage. 

She's not your "princess" for whom no man will ever be good enough. She's not your ticket out of poverty or your way out of your financially irresponsible decisions. She's not your permanent servant who must stay with you to cook and clean and sacrifice her own happiness for you. She's not your vehicle for upward social mobility, with her secular degree or her job as a doctor or engineer bringing prestige and social status to the family. 

She is your daughter, who most likely really wants to get married young and settle down early with a husband she can love. 

Don't force her to put her life on hold for you, or pressure her to fulfill YOUR childhood dreams or conform to YOUR unrealistic unattainable expectations.

As soon as a compatible, righteous Muslim man is found and approved, let her get married, grow in love, enjoy her halal relationship, and start a beautiful family! 

لقول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم: "إذا جاءكم من ترضون دينه وخلقه فأنكحوه إلا تفعلوا تكن فتنة في الأرض وفساد كبير."

Abu Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “When someone whose religion and character you are pleased with proposes to (someone under the care) of one of you, marry her off to him. If you do not do so, then there will be turmoil (Fitnah) in the land and abounding discord (Fasad).” 

[At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Maajah]

What often happens in the modern world, sadly, is that a beautiful rose goes unappreciated in its prime, unnoticed at the peak of its loveliness and fragrance and allure. Until its beauty (which should have been valued, loved, enjoyed!) starts to fade, its petals start to wither, and its leaves start to fall. Eventually, the once-beautiful hopeful rose becomes brittle and bitter, dries, and dies. Alone.

What a sad thing to witness.

Abu Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: “When someone whose religion and character you are pleased with proposes to (someone under the care) of one of you, marry her off to him. If you do not do so, then there will be turmoil (Fitnah) in the land and abounding discord (Fasad).” 

[At-Tirmidhi and Ibn Maajah]

What often happens in the modern world, sadly, is that a beautiful rose goes unappreciated in its prime, unnoticed at the peak of its loveliness and fragrance and allure. Until its beauty (which should have been valued, loved, enjoyed!) starts to fade, its petals start to wither, and its leaves start to fall. Eventually, the once-beautiful hopeful rose becomes brittle and bitter, dries, and dies. Alone.

What a sad thing to witness.
From Umm Sufyān. Join Private Group ⤵️

text:
To clarify: we do not believe that older women become “brittle”, “bitter”, or “dry up” in any literal or moral sense. That is not the point.

Older women remain valuable, virtuous, and precious in the sight of Allāh. Their worth, dignity, and honour do not diminish with age.

The rose analogy is figurative, not demeaning. It is simply illustrating a real and observable reality:

text.text: youth and physical beauty are time-sensitive assets in the context of marriage.

text: This is not a spiritual statement. It is not a moral judgement. It is a

text.text: practical reality of the marriage market.

text:
Realistically:
 • Age does matter in marriage.
 • Men, by nature, generally prefer younger women.
 • The younger a woman is, the wider her pool of potential suitors tends to be.
 • As time passes, optionality usually decreases.

Even non-Muslim societies openly acknowledge this dynamic.

The purpose of the post was

:
To encourage our sisters not to delay marriage unnecessarily, and not to sacrifice their prime years chasing things that neither guarantee happiness nor replace companionship, love, and family.

Delaying marriage often harms oneself in the long run. I have personally seen this repeatedly through the

initiative: many righteous brothers with good dīn and character will still choose a younger woman when looking for a wife, even if an older sister appears more “excellent” on paper.

A sister may seem perfect on paper, but she is 29 instead of 25, 26 instead of 23, 24 instead of 21, or 22 instead of 18 — and that alone can completely change the outcome. This is not hateful ideology; it is simply pointing out real-world behaviour.

At the same time, this does

mean:
 • Older women are inferior.
 • Older women cannot marry.
 • Older women are undeserving of love.

They absolutely are.

The message is simply this:

text.text: You are valuable at every age.
But your marital leverage is highest when you are young.
Use that wisely. Don’t delay your own happiness for illusions sold by modern culture.
This is sincere advice. Please take it, sister. Rush to marry a righteous man — this can only benefit you. Youth does not last forever.

text.text:
Mālik, from Isḥāq bni ʿAbdillāh bni Abī Ṭalḥah, from Anas bni Mālik, who said:
I went out with ʿUmar bna al-Khaṭṭāb until he entered an enclosed garden (ḥāʾiṭ).

Then I heard him say inside the garden—while a wall was between me and him—:
"ʿUmar bnu al-Khaṭṭāb, Commander of the Believers! Bakhin, bakhin! Wallāhi, you either fear Allāh, or He torments you!"
[…]
[Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr commented:] As for his saying, "Bakhin, bakhin, O Commander of the Believers", then it is a rebuke from him to his own self. And rebuking the soul and reproaching it is an act of worship, just as being pleased with it is one's demise.

text: — Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr, al-Istithkār, 8/587

:
1. حائط (ḥāʾiṭ)
Rendered as "enclosed garden", not merely "wall".

2. بخٍ بخٍ (bakhin, bakhin)
Left untranslated and transliterated. It is an exclamatory expression, here used ironically and reproachfully, not for praise. Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr explicitly clarifies this.

messages.text:
Beware—beware of software piracy and using cracked copies and the like.

All of it is theft.

The owner of the software sells it and does not consent to having it stolen and distributed for free online.

The fact that the owner may be a disbeliever does not justify stealing from him.

Also, even disbelievers consider using pirated software a breach of basic decency, and they condemn those who openly admit to it.

So, my brother, why act like this? We have no need for such thing. There is an abundance of free software—too much to count—and much of it is far better than what is sold.

Allāh will not put barakah in what you have stolen. Be certain of that.

May Allāh guide me and you.

—Abū Sahl, ʿAbdu ar-Raḥmān al-Jazāʾirī, Software Developer

text.text: Mind Expansion in a Chain of Awe

text:
Picture him, a man in rough clothes, a man who does not bend, a man with īmān strong enough to guide an ummah.

A man who led the people into victories no one expected.
A man who faced empires that thought they were eternal…

And by what means? Horses and camels. Dust and orders. Kisrā never saw it coming.

Again, picture him. A single man Allāh chose to lead the ummah. Not from a throne. Not from above. From the ground. His steps raised dust. He slept on it.

He summed it up in one line:
"We are a people Allāh honored by Islām. If we were to seek honor by other than Islām, Allāh will humiliate us".

That's ʿUmar.

Now, perhaps a thought comes to your mind. Another man…

Who casts that bigger shadow?

Abu Bakr.

Earlier. Firmer. Stronger.
He steered the ummah when it wavered, when hearts shook after the Prophet ﷺ passed.
He did not use force. He displayed certainty. And that certainty poured into every heart.

His īmān was heavier than that of the whole ummah. Yes. ʿUmar included.

ʿUmar knew and mentioned a lot how Abu Bakr was levels above him.

That is Abu Bakr.

Now, think higher still. The two of them—ministers of whom?

The Messenger of Allāh ﷺ.

Whatever greatness you felt reflecting on ʿUmar and Abu Bakr…[complete this sentence however you wish…you get the idea].

And all three were created by Allāh, عز وجل.

Think about that.

—Abū Sahl, ʿAbdurraḥmān al-Qaddārī

messages.text:
Warmth, presence, engagement—these actually signal strength.

Speak. Act. Care.

That's where character lives, not in cold silence.

Strength is not in withdrawing, but in showing up.
Not in silence, but in presence.
Not in coldness, but in care. 

Character lives where you engage, not where you hide.

Hmm... reminds of al-Albānī.

رحمة الله عليه.

He often used to tell people asking him:
"Don't be afraid of asking me anything you want, and feel free to object and tell me when you don't understand something. I'm just like you. I'm not like those sheikhs who don't allow students to raise objections".

I feel proud to be a student of his, even if in an indirect way.

—Abū Sahl, ʿAbdurraḥmān al-Qaddārī

messages.forwarded_from: عَلَىٰ نَهجِ السَّلَفِ || Upon the path of Salaf 📚
text:
بسم الله الرحمـٰن الرحيم 

Many of us often look at what we’re missing, and it makes us feel lacking — ungrateful. We remind ourselves—and one another—not to focus on what we lack, but to look at what we have. Yet how many of us truly live by this advice? Very few.

Allah ﷻ says:

﴿وَقَلِيلٌ مِّنْ عِبَادِيَ الشَّكُورُ﴾
“And very few of My servants are truly grateful.” [Sabaʾ: 13] 

We allow ourselves to feel miserable over what we do not have, while forgetting the immense blessings Allah has already bestowed upon us. And this is the nature of mankind, as Allah ﷻ says:

﴿إِنَّ الْإِنسَانَ لِرَبِّهِ لَكَنُودٌ﴾
“Indeed, man is truly ungrateful to his Lord.” [al-ʿĀdiyāt: 6]

We forget even the most obvious of blessings — health, sight, sanity, emotions, literacy — and so much more endless blessings, each of them carrying more blessings within it. The greatest of them being that Allah ﷻ guided you to Islam.

Even more than that, He guided you to Ahlus Sunnah, to Ahlul Hadith, to the manhaj of the Salaf.

How can you allow yourself to overlook all this faḍl Allah bestowed upon you? How can sadness dominate your heart when you are surrounded by so many blessings—especially the greatest of them all?

Allah has not given anyone anything greater than Islam.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

«عَلَيْكُمْ بِسُنَّتِي وَسُنَّةِ الْخُلَفَاءِ الرَّاشِدِينَ الْمَهْدِيِّينَ، عَضُّوا عَلَيْهَا بِالنَّوَاجِذِ»
“Hold firmly to my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs, bite onto it with your molar teeth" [At-Tirmidhi 2676]

But how can we cling to something we do not value? How can we hold firmly to that which we belittle or fail to recognize as a blessing? How can one truly hold onto it when they are constantly fixated on worldly matters — while overlooking this faḍl that, had Allah withheld it, they would have been among the disbelievers? And that—being cursed by Allah and cast into the Hellfire—is a calamity greater than any worldly loss. There is nothing worse than that. 

Thank Allah for what He has granted you, and hold onto it tightly, just as the Prophet ﷺ commanded you.

Allah ﷻ says:

﴿وَكَانَ فَضْلُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكَ عَظِيمًا﴾
"and ever has the favour of Allah upon you been great" [An-Nisāʾ:113]

Allah chose you—out of millions, billions, trillions of people from the beginning of time until its end—to guide you to the truth and make you among His servants.

What blessing could be greater than that?

Hold onto it firmly, because no one is guaranteed steadfastness until death. You are not promised that you will wake up tomorrow upon guidance.

The Prophet ﷺ warned us of trials so severe that a man may wake up a believer and go to sleep a disbeliever—or go to sleep a believer and wake up a disbeliever.

So ask Allah for steadfastness.

And thank Him—because if you are grateful, He will increase you:

﴿وَإِذْ تَأَذَّنَ رَبُّكُمْ لَئِن شَكَرْتُمْ لَأَزِيدَنَّكُمْ ۖ وَلَئِن كَفَرْتُمْ إِنَّ عَذَابِي لَشَدِيدٌ﴾
"And [remember] when your Lord proclaimed, 'If you are grateful, I will surely increase you [in favor]; but if you deny, indeed, My punishment is severe.'" [Ibrāhīm: 7]

The only thing that is truly worth sadness is missing out on khayr you're capable of doing. 

والله المستعان.

text_entities.text:
بسم الله الرحمـٰن الرحيم 

Many of us often look at what we’re missing, and it makes us feel lacking — ungrateful. We remind ourselves—and one another—not to focus on what we lack, but to look at what we have. Yet how many of us truly live by this advice? Very few.

Allah ﷻ says:

﴿وَقَلِيلٌ مِّنْ عِبَادِيَ الشَّكُورُ﴾
“And very few of My servants are truly grateful.” [Sabaʾ: 13] 

We allow ourselves to feel miserable over what we do not have, while forgetting the immense blessings Allah has already bestowed upon us. And this is the nature of mankind, as Allah ﷻ says:

﴿إِنَّ الْإِنسَانَ لِرَبِّهِ لَكَنُودٌ﴾
“Indeed, man is truly ungrateful to his Lord.” [al-ʿĀdiyāt: 6]

We forget even the most obvious of blessings — health, sight, sanity, emotions, literacy — and so much more endless blessings, each of them carrying more blessings within it. The greatest of them being that Allah ﷻ guided you to Islam.

Even more than that, He guided you to Ahlus Sunnah, to Ahlul Hadith, to the manhaj of the Salaf.

How can you allow yourself to overlook all this faḍl Allah bestowed upon you? How can sadness dominate your heart when you are surrounded by so many blessings—especially the greatest of them all?

Allah has not given anyone anything greater than Islam.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

«عَلَيْكُمْ بِسُنَّتِي وَسُنَّةِ الْخُلَفَاءِ الرَّاشِدِينَ الْمَهْدِيِّينَ، عَضُّوا عَلَيْهَا بِالنَّوَاجِذِ»
“Hold firmly to my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs, bite onto it with your molar teeth" [At-Tirmidhi 2676]

But how can we cling to something we do not value? How can we hold firmly to that which we belittle or fail to recognize as a blessing? How can one truly hold onto it when they are constantly fixated on worldly matters — while overlooking this faḍl that, had Allah withheld it, they would have been among the disbelievers? And that—being cursed by Allah and cast into the Hellfire—is a calamity greater than any worldly loss. There is nothing worse than that. 

Thank Allah for what He has granted you, and hold onto it tightly, just as the Prophet ﷺ commanded you.

Allah ﷻ says:

﴿وَكَانَ فَضْلُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكَ عَظِيمًا﴾
"and ever has the favour of Allah upon you been great" [An-Nisāʾ:113]

Allah chose you—out of millions, billions, trillions of people from the beginning of time until its end—to guide you to the truth and make you among His servants.

What blessing could be greater than that?

Hold onto it firmly, because no one is guaranteed steadfastness until death. You are not promised that you will wake up tomorrow upon guidance.

The Prophet ﷺ warned us of trials so severe that a man may wake up a believer and go to sleep a disbeliever—or go to sleep a believer and wake up a disbeliever.

So ask Allah for steadfastness.

And thank Him—because if you are grateful, He will increase you:

﴿وَإِذْ تَأَذَّنَ رَبُّكُمْ لَئِن شَكَرْتُمْ لَأَزِيدَنَّكُمْ ۖ وَلَئِن كَفَرْتُمْ إِنَّ عَذَابِي لَشَدِيدٌ﴾
"And [remember] when your Lord proclaimed, 'If you are grateful, I will surely increase you [in favor]; but if you deny, indeed, My punishment is severe.'" [Ibrāhīm: 7]

The only thing that is truly worth sadness is missing out on khayr you're capable of doing. 

والله المستعان.
-أم عبدالرحمـٰن السودانية غفر الله لها

messages.author: عبد الرحمن الجزائري
text:
Clarity is a form of courage. Vagueness is often a retreat.

Some people become vague when they feel intellectually challenged. Short replies. Loose words. Unfinished thoughts. Not because they are deep—because precision would expose limits.

The use of fog as protection.

This isn't wisdom. It's self-defense, against "danger".

The mind under pressure looks for exits. A release valve. Vagueness is one. If nothing clear is said, nothing clear can be questioned.

Status is preserved.
Discomfort is avoided.
Control feels intact.

But:
A confident mind clarifies.
An anxious one blurs.

Strong thinkers don't hide behind ambiguity. They define terms. They explain. They correct themselves. They engage.

Clarity costs effort, humility, but it builds.
Vagueness is cheap, because it's empty.
Do you expect value out of nothing?
Do you think clear minds, just happened to be?
Do you think clear minds did not go through clarifying situations, phases, moments, thoughts?
Exchange, give, get, surrender, take the blow. It won't kill you unless you let it.

Brevity is not the problem. Precision is what to test.

Few words can be sharp. Few words can also be evasive. One cuts. The other slips.

Real strength prefers light over fog. Presence. Accountability. Engagement.

Character shows not in how little you say—but in how clearly you're willing to be understood.

—Abū Sahl, ʿAbdurraḥmān al-Qaddārī

messages.text:
بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

First, it doesn't make sense.

Second, don't believe random posts that report "Security Breach/Exploit". If such thing existed, the experts would be all over it.

Third, I don't even use antiviruses beyond what the OS already provides. You think I'd take down my profile picture for a random post that cites no proof and no sources?

My beautiful profile picture stays as is, because if someone were to hack my channel, they wouldn't need my profile picture. It has nothing to do with that. Which should be obvious.

Would be funny if my channel gets stolen, though.

messages.author: عبد الرحمن الجزائري
messages.text:
Verily those who believe (in the Oneness of Allâh - Islâmic Monotheism) and do righteous deeds, shall have the Gardens of Al-Firdaus (Paradise) for their entertainment.

Wherein they shall dwell (forever). No desire will they have for removal therefrom.

Say (O Muhammad صلى الله عليه وسلم to mankind): If the sea were ink for (writing) the Words of my Lord, surely, the sea would be exhausted before the Words of my Lord would be finished, even if We brought (another sea) like it for its aid.

Say (O Muhammad صلى الله عليه وسلم): I am only a man like you. It has been revealed to me that your Ilâh (God) is One Ilâh (God - i.e. Allâh). So whoever hopes for the Meeting with his Lord, let him work righteousness and associate none as a partner in the worship of his Lord.

[Al-Kahf: 107-110]

Tr. Muhsin Khan and Taqi-ud-Din al-Hilali

text.text: The Rizq You Strive For and the Rizq You Wait For

text:
بســـم اللــه الرحــمــن الـرحـــيــم

The rizq you chase in this world, your material provision, is unseen, unknown, and unpredictable. Yet you wake up for it. You hustle for it. You break sweat for it. People labour day and night, and many discover that their halāl earnings still look smaller beside the glittering illusions of harām wealth.

Some over zealous women even shoulder the burden of sustaining sick parents, younger siblings, and vulnerable family members.

And still, in this dunya, the one who slows down is instantly branded “lazy,” as if humans are incapable of knowing their own intentions better than the public that judges them.

Then comes the rizq of a husband.

Suddenly, almost magically, the standards shift.

Here, passiveness becomes a badge of honour.
No looking. No searching. No asking. No initiating. No movement.
And she is never called lazy. On the contrary, she shields her inaction with the fragile umbrella of “I’m waiting for qadar,” while some so-called du‘āt applaud and clap for her “modesty,” disguising stagnancy as spirituality.

But what is she expecting, exactly?

That a husband will stroll out of the unseen?
That he will manifest like the prince charming of Snow White and Sleeping Beauty, noble, prepared, flawless, and divinely dispatched to rescue her from her own uncertainty and confused doubts?

And not an average man, no.
She imagines one strong and steadfast, with the resilience of the least of the Sahābah, a protector and provider, principled, polite, emotionally mature, well-grounded in ‘aqeedah, and firm upon the Sunnah.

But Allāh has already set the principle:

 {وَأَنْ لَيْسَ لِلْإِنسَانِ إِلَّا مَا سَعَىٰ (39) وَأَنَّ سَعْيَهُ سَوْفَ يُرَىٰ (40) ثُمَّ يُجْزَاهُ الْجَزَاءَ الْأَوْفَىٰ (41)}
“And that man can have nothing except what he strives for;
and that his striving will be seen;
then he will be fully recompensed for it.” [Surah An-Najm: 39–41]


Your delicacies of delicious meals do not appear on your dining table well arranged by miracle.

Your beautifully perfect fit clothes did not stitch themselves and cling to your body from the sky.

Your comfy shelter did not come looking for you, well situated in a good area, you sought it out, you moved toward it, you worked for it.

So why, then, should the righteous husband you desire simply knock on your door, while you wait in your living room doing shakara?

No be juju be that? Wouldn't you be sceptical?! 

The same hands that reach toward sustenance must also reach toward sincere du‘ā, and toward halāl effort, in the search for a spouse. Rizq does not descend upon those who sleep through their striving. It comes to those who walk, who move, who act, while trusting in Allāh.

Even the wife of Mūsā (before she became his wife) did not sit back and wait for destiny to unfold.
She strove, with modesty and intelligence, by suggesting to her father that he should hire Mūsā, and from that wise proposal came the marriage. She took a step, through the right channel, at the right time.

Effort through halāl avenues is not a contradiction to piety;
it is its completion.

Effort is not a betrayal of tawakkul.
Effort is the proof of it.
_
Abu Juwayriyah

messages.author: عبد الرحمن الجزائري
messages.text:
السلام عليكم ورحمة الله وبركاته،

I received an anonymous suggestion advising that when mentioning an āyah (in Arabic or English), one should precede it with "Allah said" or "قال الله تعالى", as this "was described as being from the etiquettes in order to distinguish it from one's own speech".

I appreciate the concern for proper adab with the Qur'aan.

However, this raises an important methodological point: when it is said that something is "from the etiquettes" (or any claim), we should ask: who stated this, and based on what evidence?

I looked for a scholarly statement establishing this as an etiquette and did not find one.

However, I do know that the Prophet ﷺ himself would sometimes mention āyāt in his speech without preceding them with "قال الله تعالى", such as in Khuṭbat al-Ḥājah, in his letter to Qayṣar, and in the narration in al-Bukhārī (7451) where he recited: { وما قدروا الله حق قدره }.

Likewise, when reading the works of scholars, one finds that they often cite āyāt directly within explanation without consistently preceding them with that phrase.

In the recent post (likely) in question, the āyāt were written clearly, bracketed, numbered, and accompanied by their sūrah reference and recitation, without any of my own speech mixed in. There was no ambiguity requiring further distinction.

This serves as a useful reminder that when a claim is made — especially in religious matters — it is important to verify it, ask for evidence, and distinguish between established rulings, recommended practices, and personal stylistic preferences.

هذا، والله أعلم.
جزاكم الله خيرا.

text.text: Do Not Apologize for Asking About Knowledge

text:
I was asked by someone about a point of knowledge who then said: I apologize for the disturbance.

So I told him:

text.text:
My son, do not apologize for asking, for asking about knowledge is not a disturbance, rather it is a path to guidance and elevation.

Whoever asks in order to learn has done well, and whoever is asked and answers is rewarded. 

Thus, do not feel embarrassed and reach out whenever you need to, and know that this excessive ḥayā (shyness) may be from shaytān to turn you from goodness.

- Written by Sheikh Faiṣal al-Ḥāshidi وفقه الله
Tr: umm Tamīm as-Ṣūmāliyyah

messages.author: عبد الرحمن الجزائري
text: : Some people think LLM chatbots are garbage, and some think they are a dream come true. Why?

text.text:
Because humans don’t evaluate tools. They evaluate expectations.

An LLM is not magic. It’s not conscious. It’s not “thinking.” It’s a probabilistic pattern engine trained on absurd amounts of text. It predicts the next token given context. That’s it. No consciousness. No inner awareness. Just math.

Now here’s where things get spicy.
If someone expects: – perfect factual authority
– consistent reasoning
– deep understanding
– accountability
They will eventually hit hallucinations, logical slips, overconfidence. And they’ll say: “This is garbage.”

They expected a sage. They got a parrot in a suit.

If someone expects: – autocomplete on steroids
– idea generator
– drafting assistant
– research starting point
– thought sparring partner
They’ll say: “This is insane. Magic.”
Same tool. Different mental model.

There’s also psychology involved. Humans anthropomorphize easily. When something speaks fluently, we assign it mind. That’s a cognitive shortcut. We project agency where there is none. The smoother the language, the stronger the illusion.

Another layer: competence illusion. When a system speaks confidently, people assume correctness. Confidence is not accuracy. Humans do this to each other too. Same bug, new substrate.
And then there’s power asymmetry. If someone uses it passively, asking it to “think for me,” it will disappoint them. If someone uses it actively—challenging, verifying, steering—it becomes a force multiplier. The difference is epistemic discipline.

Think of it like fire. Fire can cook your food or burn your house. The fire isn’t magical or useless. It depends on how well you understand combustion.
LLMs amplify the user. They don’t replace cognition. They extend it. Sometimes beautifully. Sometimes catastrophically.

The real divide isn’t about the model.
It’s about how well the human understands what it is.

text:
I hope this clarifies the technology and confusion.
Since it's a widespread tool, we should learn about it, at least to be safe from its cons.

messages.text:
الشيخ الألباني رحمه الله وقوة حجته في المناظرة.

الشيخ سليمان الرحيلي

تفريغ:

وأَنَا أُحِبُّ أَنْ أَسْمَعَ كَلَامَ الشَّيْخِ كَثِيرًا.
لِأَنَّ الشَّيْخَ الْأَلْبَانِيَّ رَحِمَهُ اللهُ وَاسِعُ الْحِفْظِ لِلْأَدِلَّةِ قَوِيُّ الْحُجَّةِ.
تَسْتَفِيدُ مِنْ سَمَاعِ أَشْرِطَتِهِ.
فَوْقَ الْعِلْمِ الْغَزِيرِ: الْقُدْرَةُ عَلَى الْمُنَاظِرَةِ، فَهُوَ مِنْ أَقْوَى النَّاسِ فِي الْمُنَاظَرَةِ.
وَإِنِّي كُنْتُ أُرْفُقُ كَثِيرًا بِكُلِّ مَنْ يُنَاظِرُ الشَّيْخَ الْأَلْبَانِيَّ.
صَعْبٌ أَنْ يُنَاظَرَ، لِقُوَّةِ حُجَّتِهِ وَقُدْرَتِهِ عَلَى الاِسْتِنْباطِ.
اسْتِنْبَاطَاتٍ مِنَ الْكَلَامِ تَجْعَلُ الْمُنَاظِرَ لَا يَسْتَطِيعُ أَنْ يَسْتَمِرَّ فِي الْمُنَاظَرَةِ.
وَهَذَا لِسِعَةِ حِفْظِهِ رَحِمَهُ اللهُ رَحْمَةً وَاسِعَةً.
وَاللهُ أَنْعَمَ عَلَى الْأُمَّةِ بِعُلَمَاءِ أَفْذَاذ، عَبْرَ تَارِيخِهَا، وَلَمْ يَنْقَطِعْ هَذَا بِحَمْدِ اللَّهِ.
وَالْخَيْرُ لِلْأُمَّةِ أَنْ تُحِبَّ عُلَمَاءَهَا.
وَأَنْ تَعْرِفَ لَهُمْ فَضْلَهُمْ.
مِنْ غَيْرِ تَعَصُّبٍ لِأَحَدٍ.
وَمِنْ غَيْرِ رَدِّ الْحَقِّ مِنْ أَجْلِ أَحَدٍ.
وَإِنَّمَا يُعْرَفُ فَضْلُ الْعُلَمَاءِ وَتُقْرَأُ سِيَرُهُمْ وَيَسْتَفِيدُ طُلَّابُ الْعِلْمِ مِنْ قِرَاءَةِ سِيَرِهِمْ.

وَيُنْشُرُ فَضْلَهُمْ.

وَيَنْصُرُ الْحَقَّ.
قَالَهُ قَرِيبٌ أَوْ بَعِيدٌ.

text.text: Shaykh al-Albānī, may Allāh have mercy on him, and the strength of his argumentation

I love listening to the shaykh often, because ash-shaykh al-Albānī, may Allāh have mercy on him, possessed a vast memory of evidences and formidable skill in argumentation. Listening to his recordings is immensely beneficial.

Beyond his deep knowledge, he had an exceptional ability for debate, making him one of the strongest in argumentation. I used to feel for anyone debating ash-shaykh al-Albānī, for it is difficult to contend with him due to the strength of his reasoning and his skill in drawing precise conclusions.

His insights in discussion could leave an opponent unable to continue, which is a testament to the breadth of his memory, may Allāh have mercy on him abundantly.

Allāh has blessed the ummah throughout history with exceptional scholars, and this blessing continues, ḥamd be to Allāh. The good for the Ummah is to love its scholars and recognize their virtues—without fanaticism toward anyone, nor by denying the truth for anyone’s sake.

The virtue of scholars is known through their biographies, and knowledge seekers benefit from studying them. 

Their virtues are to be spread.

Al-ḥaqq is to be supported, whether said by someone close or distant.

messages.author: عبد الرحمن الجزائري
messages.text:
الإمام الألباني.
هذا يا إخوة من أئمة الدنيا في هذا الزمان.
إمام في التوحيد والسنة والفقه. يخطئ ويصيب. لكنه إمام.
حبه من دين الله، كسائر علماء أهل السنة.
والله من قرأ سيرته يحتقر نفسه مهما بذل لدين الله.
رجل بذل حياته كلها لخدمة دين الله.
يبقى في المكتبة منذ أن تفتح في أول أول من يدخل، ويبقى إلى آخر من يخرج حتى تغلق المكتبة.
على كبر سنه يقف على السلم يفتش في المخطوطات.
ما هو في الفهارس والمكتبة الشاملة—ويقول طالب علم.
ويجلس المجالس الطويلة يبين السنة، ويناظر أهل البدع، ويرد البدع.
مثل هؤلاء العلماء قد تجاوزوا القنطرة، والله ما يقع فيه أحد على سبيل الوقيعة إلا وهو على ضلال.
أما التخطيئة والتصويبة والتصويب، فكل العلماء يخطئون ويصيبون.
ترد الرأي وتبين أنه غلط، طيب، لكن الوقيعة في أعراض هؤلاء العلماء والطعن فيهم والسعي أن تستخرج كلمات في الطعن فيهم، والله نذير شؤم.
وما أعرف أحدا اتخذ هذا الطريق ووفقَه الله. أبدا!

ترد الرأي وتبين أنه غلط، طيب، لكن الوقيعة في أعراض هؤلاء العلماء والطعن فيهم والسعي أن تستخرج كلمات في الطعن فيهم، والله نذير شؤم.
وما أعرف أحدا اتخذ هذا الطريق ووفقَه الله. أبدا!

messages.author: عبد الرحمن الجزائري
text:
This, my brothers, is one of the leading imāms of the world in this era.

An imām in Tawḥīd, the Sunnah, and fiqh. He can be mistaken and he can be correct, but he is an imām.

Loving him is from the religion of Allāh, like the rest of the scholars of Ahl as-Sunnah.

Wallāhi, whoever studies his biography belittles themselves, no matter what they have offered for the religion of Allāh.

He devoted his entire life to serving the religion of Allāh.

He would remain in the library from the moment it opened—being among the first to enter—and stay until the last person left and the library closed.

Despite his advanced age, he would stand on a ladder examining manuscripts.

He didn't have indexes and al-Maktabah ash-Shāmilah (and yet some call themselves "knowledge seekers").
He would sit through long sessions explaining the Sunnah, debating the people of innovation, and refuting their innovations.

Scholars like these have surpassed al-qanṭarah [meaning their status is unquestionable]; Wallāhi, no one slanders him and is not a deviant.

As for correction and rectification, all scholars could be right and wrong. You reject the opinion and correct it—that is fine.

But to attack the character of these scholars, to malign them, and to seek words to disparage them—Wallāhi, this is a harbinger of misfortune.

I do not know anyone who has taken this path and been granted success by Allāh. Never!

text: Shaykh al-Islām explained in Darʿ Taʿāruḍ al-ʿAql wa an-Naql (1/ 20-21):

text.text: ...And since clarifying the intention of the Messenger ﷺ in these matters cannot be properly accomplished except by refuting rational objections, while refraining from placing this refutation in opposition to the texts of the Prophets, we have explained in this book the corruption of the corrupt law by which people were turned away from the path of Allāh and from understanding the Messenger’s intention and affirming what he conveyed. For any proof established to clarify the Messenger’s intention is of no benefit if a decisive rational objection is assumed to contradict it; rather, it becomes a point of discrediting the Messenger, and a point of discrediting against those who rely upon his words. This is like the condition of a sick person whose body contains corrupt humors that prevent him from benefiting from food — the food cannot nourish him while the corrupt humors are present and spoil it. Likewise, the heart that believes a decisive rational proof establishes the negation of the Attributes [of Allāh], or some of them, or the negation of the universality of His creation of everything, or the negation of His command and prohibition, or the impossibility of the Resurrection, or other such matters — reasoning from the Qurʾān and Sunnah in these cases is of no benefit to them...

text:
How do we solve such problem? By repeating the texts of prohibition over and over?

No.

Consider the solution of Shaykh al-Islām:

text.text:
…Reasoning from the Qurʾān and Sunnah is of no benefit in this matter except when the invalidity of the opposing argument has been clarified.
The invalidity of that opposing argument may be known both in general and in detail.
As for the general [knowledge]: one who has complete faith in Allāh and His Messenger, who knows the Messenger’s intention with certainty and affirms what he conveyed, and who knows that any argument opposing this is a refuted argument akin to sophistical reasoning — as Allāh, Exalted is He, says:
"And those who dispute concerning Allâh (His religion of Islâmic Monotheism with which Muhammad, salla-llāhu ʿalayhi wa sallam, has been sent), after it has been accepted (by the people), of no use is their dispute before their Lord and on them is wrath, and for them will be a severe torment". [Ash-Shūrā: 16]
As for the detailed [knowledge]: it consists in knowing the invalidity of the opposing argument in particular…

text: An effective remedy addresses the core cause, not the symptoms.

text:
Al-Imām Ibn al-Qayyim رحمه الله says:

"Complaining to Him—Glorified is He—does not contradict beautiful patience. Rather, the servant turning away from complaining to anyone else entirely, and directing his complaint solely to Him,

Allāh—Glorified is He—tests His servant to hear his complaint, his pleading, and his supplication. He has condemned those who do not humble themselves before Him and do not submit to Him at the time of trial, as He said:

﴾And indeed We seized them with punishment, but they did not humble themselves to their Lord, nor did they invoke (Allāh) with submission to Him.﴿ 
[Surat Al-Mu'minūn: 76]

The servant is too weak to pretend to be patient and self-sufficient before his Lord. The Lord—Exalted is He—does not want His servant to pretend patience before Him. Rather, He wants him to submit and plead to Him. He—Exalted is He—detests the one who complains about Him to His creation, and He loves the one who complains of his condition to Him."

'Uddat aṣ-Ṣābirīn wa dhakhīrat ash-Shākirīn (Page 63)'

السلام عليكم ورحمة الله وبركاته،

موقع جديد دروس جامع مسائل العقيدة الصحيحة، للأستاذ فيصل بن مسفر الزنامي الوادعي

موقع سريع وبسيط للاستماع لجميع الدروس في مكان واحد.

ماذا يقدم لك الموقع؟

*

: يعود بك الموقع لنفس الثانية التي توقفت عندها في كل درس تلقائياً.

*

: العثور على أي درس برقم الدرس أو العنوان أو النبذة فوراً.

*

: إمكانية تسريع أو تبطئ الصوت حسب حاجتك.

*

: يتم جلب الدروس الجديدة آلياً من قناة الشيخ.

*

: إضافة تفريغ نصي للدروس، إن شاء الله.

رابط الموقع:

برمجت الموقع ليكون آليا ولا أحتاج للعمل عليه مرة أخرى، لأتفرغ لغيره، وقد استعملت في ذلك جيميناي.

والحمد لله رب العالمين. لولا توفيق الله، لما عملت مثل هذا.

text.text: Do Not Do The Thinking For Him

text:
💭☁️

The child was not created empty.

He was created with a mind that completes what it does not see, and builds what does not exist in front of him.

Give him a stick, and it becomes a horse. 🌿
Give him a stone, and it becomes treasure. 💎
Give him nothing, and he creates a world. 🌍

This is not a defect. This is the mind working as it was designed.

But when you give him ready-made images for everything, you close the doors he was meant to open. 🚪

There is nothing left to complete. Nothing left to imagine. Nothing left to build. ⛔️

He becomes a receiver, not a creator.

Like the one who relies on a calculator for every small sum, until he can no longer calculate without it. 🧮

The tool did not increase his ability. It replaced it.

Images do the same.

They give the answer before the question is formed.❓
They give the form before the mind searches for it. 🔍

And a mind that does not search, weakens.

Protect his imagination. 🛡

Do not rush to fill his world with finished pictures.

Leave space for him to see what is not there. ⬜️

That space is where the mind grows. 🌱

—Abū Sahl ʿAbdurraḥmān al-Qaddārī (who used to turn sticks into horses and run around the house making horse noises)

text: A possible explanation:

text.text:
This phrase suggests that hardships are a form of training. It implies that you may not yet have the strength, character, or wisdom to handle the blessings you've prayed for. The hardship acts as a preparation phase—refining your patience or skills—so that when the relief arrives, you are actually ready to sustain and appreciate it.

​Essentially: The delay isn't a "no", it's a "not yet; you're still growing".

text:
I suspected that, and it seems like the only possible meaning.
والله أعلم.

May Allāh reward you all, especially who offered possible explanations.

messages.text:
Question: Is it better to translate "غيب" as "unseen" or "unwitnessed"?

Answer: "Unwitnessed" is better, because in Arabic, "غيب" and "شهادة" refer to "witnessing" or "testimony", not simply "seeing".

So, "unseen" is flat and narrow for "غيب".

messages.text:
Question: Is it better to translate "طالب علم" as "Student of knowledge" or "Knowledge seeker"?

Answer: "Knowledge seeker".
"طلب":
in Arabic is not "studying", it's "seeking".
"Studying" is "دراسة".

To seek knowledge is deeper than just studying it. It conveys drive, will, persistence, a goal.
"Studying" gives it an academic taste, which is...meh.

text.text:
س (1227) مَا هُوَ سَيِّدُ الِاسْتِغْفَارِ؟
جـ (1227) اللَّهُمَّ أَنْتَ رَبِّي، لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا أَنْتَ، خَلَقْتَنِي وَأَنَا عَبْدُكَ، وَأَنَا عَلَى عَهْدِكَ وَوَعْدِكَ مَا اسْتَطَعْتُ، أَعُوذُ بِكَ مِنْ شَرِّ مَا صَنَعْتُ، أَبُوءُ لَكَ بِنِعْمَتِكَ عَلَيَّ، وَأَبُوءُ لَكَ بِذَنْبِي فَاغْفِرْ لِي؛ فَإِنَّهُ لَا يَغْفِرُ الذُّنُوبَ إِلَّا أَنْتَ.

Q (1227) What is Sayyid al-Istighfār?
A (1227) "Allāhumma anta Rabbī, lā ilāha illā Anta, khalaqtanī wa-anā ʿabduka, wa-anā ʿalā ʿahdika wa-waʿdika mā istaṭaʿtu. Aʿūthu bika min sharri mā ṣanaʿtu. Abūʾu laka biniʿmatika ʿalayya, wa-abūʾu laka bithanbī fa-ghfir lī; fa-innahu lā yaghfiru ath-thunūba illā Anta" (O Allāh, You are my Lord; there is no god except You. You created me and I am Your slave, and I remain upon Your covenant and promise as much as I am able. I seek refuge in You from the evil of what I have done. I acknowledge before You Your favor upon me, and I acknowledge my sin to You, so forgive me; for none forgives sins except You).

text:
Source: Kanz al-Aṭfāl.

لا إله إلا الله.
حلاوة هذا الدعاء لا توصف.

Note: the translation is deliberate. Each term is picked after careful review. Just in case you find some of my choices don't get along with the common view.

text:
I suggest translating "سيد" as "chief".

Not "boss", not "head", not "president", none of that.

Because "chief" doesn't necessarily convey ruling. It is also used to mean status and position, which fits perfectly.
الحمد لله.

For example, if you want to say
الحسن والحسين سيدا شباب الجنة.

There is no leadership or ruling in al-Jannah. That ḥadīth means they are of the highest rank. "Chief" works here amazingly. الحمد لله.
